title: Plasticity
content_html:
Plasticity

Neuroplasticity is the ability of neural circuits to change their structure and function in response to experience, activity, or injury. It’s the fundamental property that allows us to learn, remember, and adapt. When two neurons repeatedly fire together, the synapse between them strengthens. More receptors (like AMPA receptors for glutamate) are added to the postsynaptic neuron, so the signal passes more easily in the future. This is often called “Hebbian learning” → cells that fire together wire together. The opposite process describes how synapses that are rarely used weaken over time, pruning connections that aren’t useful. These processes alter how efficiently information travels across the network.

Entire brain regions can reassign functions if another region is damaged, for example, after a stroke, nearby areas (or even the opposite hemisphere) can sometimes take over lost functions through training and rehab. In sensory deprivation (e.g. blindness), the visual cortex can be repurposed to process touch or sound. Plasticity is the brain’s way of rewriting its own “code” - by adjusting connection strengths, creating new links, and repurposing circuits - allowing finite biological matter to generate flexible, evolving memory and consciousness.

When you experience something (say, seeing a friend), specific neural circuits fire. Synaptic plasticity strengthens the links between neurons that were co-active, and the pattern of strengthened synapses becomes the engraved trace (sometimes called an engram). Without plasticity, every event would “pass through” without leaving a mark. Over time, strengthened synapses are consolidated: proteins are made, spines stabilized, and circuits reorganized. Sleep plays a major role - hippocampal “replay” drives plastic changes in the cortex, moving memories into long-term storage. Plasticity at the structural level (new spines, pruning unused ones) shapes which traces persist and which fade.

Remembering is essentially reactivating the same circuits that were modified during encoding. Plasticity means that recall isn’t static: every time you retrieve a memory, the circuit becomes labile and can be updated - a process called reconsolidation, which explains why memories can distort over time: plasticity re-writes, it doesn’t just “read out.”

Episodic memory and imagination use overlapping circuits (hippocampus, default mode network). Plasticity in these networks allows not only storing the past but re-combining fragments into simulations of possible futures; this is why your sense of “future memories” feels similar to recalling the past. Plasticity isn’t just a background feature - it is the mechanism that makes memory possible.

How is all this possible?

Neurons are specialized cells whose main job is to send and receive electrical signals. They do this through ion channels (proteins embedded in the cell membrane) that let charged particles (sodium, potassium, calcium, chloride) flow in and out. These flows generate voltage changes (action potentials) that travel down axons and trigger neurotransmitter release at synapses. At the micro-level, it’s chemistry and physics. But the pattern of activity across billions of neurons encodes information.

Synapses are not static wires; they are dynamic junctions where the strength of transmission can change. Plasticity happens when activity patterns alter receptor density (more AMPA receptors inserted into the postsynaptic membrane), release probability of neurotransmitters and spine growth or shrinkage (structural remodeling). Proteins act as the “molecular machinery” carrying out these changes. Proteins and chemicals don’t “know” about memory. But their rules of interaction let networks adapt.

One neuron firing doesn’t mean much. But ~86 billion neurons, each with up to 10,000 synapses, create an astronomical number of possible states. Out of these patterns, stable ensembles form (engrams) - like fingerprints of experience. Memory is not “stored” in a molecule like a file on a disk, but in the relational state of a huge network. Conscious memory emerges not from any single molecule, but from the coordination of billions of physical events over time, which is similar to how “life” emerges from cells, or “wetness” emerges from H₂O molecules. The whole is more than the parts. This flexibility, scaled up, creates networks that can encode, store, and reconstruct experiences. Memory is not in the molecules - it’s in the patterns their interactions make possible.
